preamble: Loss of pharyngealization in the emphatic voiced stop [dˤ], which merges with plain [d]. Medieval Maltese inherited three contrastive emphatic obstruents from Arabic, ṭ, ḍ and ṣ; Judaeo-Maltese notarial documents in Hebrew script write them with three distinct Hebrew letters, ض being rendered by ṣade with a diacritic (Wettinger 1985, cited by Puech 2018). In late medieval Maltese the contrast between emphatic and plain consonants was lost, and stem vowels took over the lexical contrasts: stems whose Arabic etymon had an emphatic have the stem vowel a (Puech 2018). Puech's inventory of medieval Maltese has no separate ẓ, and Modern Maltese d also continues Arabic ẓāʾ ظ (dell 'shade' < ظِلّ, Wiktionary). Word-initially the result is plain [d], as in dawl /dawl/ 'light' from Arabic ضَوْء (Wiktionary); word-finally it is devoiced like any Maltese final obstruent (marid /maˈriːt/ 'ill' < مَرِيض). The ṭ and ṣ halves of the same merger are filed under [tˤ] > [t] and [sˤ] > [s]. Juba Arabic likewise keeps only the plain member of each plain/emphatic pair (Wikipedia, Juba Arabic). Classical Arabic ḍād is reconstructed as a lateral [ɮˤ]; its change to the stop [dˤ] is filed as an earlier, separate step.
